I’ve considered many avenues to pursue with my final post here. I have many desires, but only so much time. So, I have decided to make one last post about Stoicism and what it means to me.

So why am I writing this? This is my farewell and thank you to the Voat community. This community has been such a blessing to me personally. I spent years lurking and contributed little, and I saw a void. There was very little discussion of philosophy or improvement. It was generally complaining and wallowing, or simple anger. I had been reading Marcus Aurelius, and I decided to share my journey. I hadn’t studied philosophy since college, but I thought others could benefit from the things I was learning. The response was overwhelming, and that response is what kept me going. I began sharing my daily aphorisms, and many began to participate in the discussion. I honestly learned more than I taught, especially at the beginning, and I am incredibly grateful to everyone who has helped me out along the way.

Now to the actual post. What do I want to leave you with? Simple. The Four Virtues of Stoicism.

• Wisdom
• Courage
• Temperance
• Justice

Anyone can look them up and figure out what each word is defined as, but what do they mean to you? And for this post, what do they mean to me?

Wisdom

Wisdom to me is about knowing. Knowing how to tell just from unjust. Good from evil. Right from wrong. The trustworthy from the charlatans. And knowing where you want to go.

If one does not know to which port he sails, no wind is favorable.

-Seneca

How can you know what the best course of action is if you don’t have a plan? How can you know what preparations need to be made if you don’t even understand what outcome you are hoping for?

But also realize that there isn’t a man among us who knows everything. Every person is ignorant in their own ways, and it is different for each of us as our lives have lead us here via different paths. There is a passage in Plato’s Apology that is quite famous and deserves much consideration. It is a quote from Socrates:

Well, I am certainly wiser than this man. It is only too likely that neither of us has any knowledge to boast of; but he thinks that he knows something which he does not know, whereas I am quite conscious of my ignorance.

-Socrates, Plato’s Apology

The wise know they are ignorant, while a fool thinks he knows all. Every single person you meet will have more knowledge and wisdom than you in certain areas. And you will be wiser and more knowledgeable in other areas. Put your pride aside and realize this, but do not be overly humble. Be self-aware. However, you need to be able to recognize a fool who thinks himself wise.

A wise man will have an idea of the best course of action, but he will always be willing to accept suggestions. Do not be blinded by your pride. You are not infallible. Know this, and you will begin your path to wisdom.

Courage

In a word: Bravery. While it seems simple, courage is a complex topic. Many like to define it as overcoming fear (the old adage “there cannot be courage without fear” comes to mind), but Stoicism also teaches that fear is illogical as it is simply worry about the future, and we have no control over what happens in the future, merely how we will respond. So I think courage deserves a solid definition.

To me, courage is about having the testicular fortitude to do what is right in the face of danger. Do lay your life on the line for what you believe. To nut up or shut up. Not eloquent, so allow me to lean on another quote, though it may be from an unexpected source this time:

Life is a storm, my young friend. You will bask in the sunlight one moment, be shattered on the rocks the next. What makes you a man is what you do when that storm comes. You must look into that storm and shout as you did in Rome. Do your worst, for I will do mine! Then the fates will know you as we know you

-Alexandre Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo

Courage is about facing the avalance and saying, “come on then.” Being brave enough to do what is right on a daily basis is fairly easy and simple. Courage is doing it in the hardest of times. That is why courage is the most important of the four virtues for our future. We are facing the hardest of times, will we have the courage to fight? Will we be brave, or will we roll over and die like a beaten dog? Make your ancestors proud. Do something your descendants will thank you for. Do your worst, for I will do mine.

Temperance

Courage may be the most important virtue for the future, but temperance is the most important now. We have thrown temperance to the wayside and given in to our base desires as a society. It is not my intention to get into the reasons we have arrived here, but to help prepare my fellow men for wha tis to come.

Forgetting temperance has been the downfall of many societies, including our own. We live decadent lives of luxury and ease. We never know fear, cold, or hunger. We want for nothing and we lack for nothing. We are soft. We are weak. We must do better.

Do you need that 75” television? Do you need that new laptop? Do you need a new truck? No. None of it. It is not necessary for life, and it should be treated as such. Most importantly, we waste our time by selling it for money to buy shit we don’t need. Perhaps we need to back up and lead simpler lives. Spend a week in the woods with no electronics and find out what you actually need in life.

Wealth consists not in having great possessions, but in having few wants.

-Epictetus

Temperance isn’t only about getting rid of that which is unnecessary however, it is also about self-control. This is the true sin of modern man, lack of self-control.

Ask yourself at every moment, ‘Is this necessary’

-Marcus Aurelius

Do you need to masturbate? Do you need to drink? Do you need to smoke? Why are you doing these things if they are unnecessary? Are you such a child that you cannot control your desires and act with restraint? I cannot claim victory in this area myself as I am also a sinner, but the first step is recognizing the problem.

When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.

-1 Corinthians 13:11

Put away your childish tendencies. Become a man who is in control of his emotions and desires.

This is the virtue that got me into Stoicism. I saw myself becoming weak. I gave into my desires wantonly. I was on a self-destructive spiral that would inevitably led to my divorce and death. I didn’t care. I was ashamed, angry, distant, drunk, aloof, uncaring. I was depressed by what I thought should have been a better life, not realizing how good it was. I was an observer in my own life, and I didn’t care. I was a fucking disgrace.

And then, I was saved. Not in the religious sense, but in a more real sense. My wife woke me up to my self-destructive path and made me acknowledge what was happening. And when I couldn’t hide from it anymore, I decided to confront it head-on. I attacked my reckless behavior. And then I stumbled upon Meditations. It wasn’t quick, but over time I regained control. I have never discussed it here, but I have had a drinking problem in the past. I am not an alcoholic, I was just bored. Now I am able to have a drink and control myself without worrying about spiraling out of control because I have learned temperance. I can control my anger and act with discipline and logic.

I have used the word quite a few times, and it is apt for temperance: CONTROL. That is what it is all about, being in control of oneself while understanding that things that happen around us are out of our control. And being wise enough to know the difference between the two.

God, grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change,

courage to change the things I can,

and wisdom to know the difference.

Justice

Justice is the source of all other virtues

...speak the truth, frankly and without evasions, and act as you should – and as other people deserve.

-Marcus Aurelius

To me, justice is akin to integrity. Doing what is right because it is right, especially when nobody is looking.

Justice is difficult for me to define. Is it doing what is right? Yes, but who decides what is right? Each of us. And what if we disagree on what is right? Then one of us will feel an injustice has been done. This is something that each of us have to decide for ourselves, “what is right?” And what do we do if our enemies decide their action is just, and ours is evil? This goes back beyond Stoicism to the beginning of philosophy. My answer? You will know it when you see it. It is hard to define right and wrong, but we KNOW right from wrong. We know when an injustice has been committed, and injustice is wrong.

To do an injustice is to do yourself an injustice – it degrades you. And you can also commit injustice by doing nothing.

-Marcus Aurelius

There is an inordinate amount of injustice in the world, yet we do nothing to stop it. We allow injustice to exist, and therefore we allow evil. In this way, we ourselves become evil. Why do we allow it to continue?

The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.

-Edmund Burke

Let us balance life’s books each day. The one who puts the finishing touches on their life each day is never short of time.

-Seneca
